13.9 Solutions to Exercises 9 - Exercises on the orbit stabiliser theorem and the orbit counting theorem Solution. (Question 9.5.1) A set of orbit representatives is {1, 4, 7}. This is because: G1 = {1, 2, 3}, G4 = {4, 5, 6}, and G7 = {7, 8, 9}. These are all disjoint, so X = G1 ∪ G4 ∪ G7 is a way of writing X as a disjoint union of orbits. Of course you might also write X = G2 ∪ G4 ∪ G8, etc. [You definitely can’t write G1 ∪ G2 ∪ G4 ∪ G8 because G1 and G2 are not disjoint.] Solution. (Question 9.5.2) This is an easy application of the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem, which states that for all x in a G-set X we have, ∣Gx∣ = [G ∶ StabG(x)]. When G is finite we can do even better: ∣Gx∣ = ∣G∣ / ∣StabG(x)∣. (a) Here ∣Gx∣ = 4 and ∣G∣ = 20. Plugging in gives ∣StabG(x)∣ = 5. (b) Since ∣G∣ = 20 and ∣StabG(y)∣ = 2, we have ∣Gy∣ = 10. Solution. (Question 9.5.3) If you draw out a pentagon and label its corners, you will see that the orbit under D10 of the corner 1 is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} so the action is transitive. We also have that the stabiliser of corner 1 in D10 is {e, (2 5)(3 4)}. Plugging all this into the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem gives, ∣D101∣ = ∣{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}∣ = 5 = 10 2 = ∣D10∣ ∣StabD10 (1)∣ = [D10 ∶ StabD10 (1)]. Thus, the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem holds in this case. Solution. (Question 9.5.4) Suppose Y is an orbit and x ∈ Y . Since Y is an orbit we have Y = Gy for some y ∈ X. Therefore x = λ(g)y for some g ∈ G. This implies that y = λ(g−1)x. Note that for all h ∈ G we have λ(h)x = λ(h)λ(g)y = λ(hg)y ∈ Gy. Hence Gx ⊆ Gy. On the other hand, for all h ∈ G we have λ(h)y = λ(h)λ(g−1)x = λ(hg−1)x ∈ Gx. Hence Gy ⊆ Gx. Therefore, Gx = Gy = Y . Solution. (Question 9.5.5) The elements in A7 that fix 1 are the elements of the stabiliser StabA7 (1). So, this question requires just an easy application of the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem. We know (because A7 is transitive) that the orbit A71 is equal to X. Thus, 7 = ∣A71∣ = ∣A7∣ / ∣StabA7 (1)∣ = 7!/2 ∣StabA7 (1)∣ . Rearranging gives ∣StabA7 (1)∣ = (7!/2)/7 = 360. Solution. (Question 9.5.6) Fix x, y ∈ X. Since G acts transitively on X, we know that Gx = X = Gy, and so importantly ∣Gx∣ = ∣Gy∣. Since G is a finite group, we know by the Orbit-Stabiliser Theorem that, ∣G∣ ∣StabG(x)∣ = ∣Gx∣ = ∣Gy∣ = ∣G∣ ∣StabG(y)∣ . Therefore, ∣StabG(x)∣ = ∣StabG(y)∣.

(Question 9.5.7) We list all elements in S4 and the elements of Y that they fix. g ∈ S4 FixY(g) ∣FixY(g)∣ e Y 16 (1 2) {(i, j) ∶ i, j ∈ {3, 4}} 4 (1 3) {(i, j) ∶ i, j ∈ {2, 4}} 4 (1 4) {(i, j) ∶ i, j ∈ {2, 3}} 4 (2 3) {(i, j) ∶ i, j ∈ {1, 4}} 4 (2 4) {(i, j) ∶ i, j ∈ {1, 3}} 4 (3 4) {(i, j) ∶ i, j ∈ {1, 2}} 4 (1 2 3) {(4, 4)} 1 (1 3 2) {(4, 4)} 1 (1 2 4) {(3, 3)} 1 (1 4 2) {(3, 3)} 1 (1 3 4) {(2, 2)} 1 (1 4 3) {(2, 2)} 1 (2 3 4) {(1, 1)} 1 (2 4 3) {(1, 1)} 1 (1 2 3 4) ∅ 0 (1 3)(2 4) ∅ 0 (1 4 3 2) ∅ 0 (1 2 4 3) ∅ 0 (1 4)(2 3) ∅ 0 (1 3 4 2) ∅ 0 (1 3 2 4) ∅ 0 (1 2)(3 4) ∅ 0 (1 4 2 3) ∅ 0 Now apply the Orbit Counting Theorem: the number of orbits is 1 24 (16 + 4 ⋅ 6 + 1 ⋅ 8) = 2. Solution. (Question 9.5.8) Recall that the regular action is λ(g)h = gh for all g ∈ G and for all h ∈ G. Now for all g ∈ G we have that h ∈ FixG(g) ⟺ λ(g)h = h ⟺ gh = h ⟺ g = eG. Therefore, if g /= eG then FixG(g) = ∅. Of course FixG(eG) = G. Applying the Orbit Counting Theorem we therefore have, # orbits = 1 ∣G∣ ∑ g∈G ∣FixG(g)∣ = 1 ∣G∣ (∣G∣ + 0 + Π + 0) = ∣G∣ ∣G∣ = 1. Thus, there is only one orbits so the action is transitive. Solution. (Question 9.5.9) As noted in the hint, this question is equivalent to asking: how many octagons with corners coloured white/black are there with precisely 3 corners coloured black, if we consider two such octagons to be the same if one can be transformed into the other by an element of D16. Using the analysis we saw in lectures, we let Y be the set of all octagons whose corners are coloured white/black in such a way that precisely 3 corners on each octagon are black. Then ∣Y ∣ = (8 3) = 56. We need a sensible way of thinking about the elements of Y , so let’s list the corner colours (starting from the top and working anticlockwise) as an 8-tuple. For example, the octagon shown in the hint for this question is (b,b,w,w,w,w,b,w). Now D16 acts on Y in the obvious way: the rotation ρ (by 360/8 degrees anticlockwise) sends (b, b, w, w, w, b, w) to (w, b, b, w, w, w, b), and so on. We first note that ρ, ρ2, . . . , ρ7 all fix no element in Y (you should draw some diagrams to convince yourself this is true). Thus, ∣FixY(ρi)∣ = 0 for i = 1, 2, . . . , 7.

As noted in lectures, D16 contains two types of reflections: four whose line of symmetry is through a corner (let’s call these σ1, σ2, σ3, σ4), and four whose line of symmetry is through an edge (let’s call these σ5, σ6, σ7, σ8). Consider σ1 and some element y of Y . If the two corners that the line of symmetry passes through are both white or both black, then y cannot be fixed by σ1 (because one side of the line of symmetry has too many black corners). On the other hand, if precisely one of the corners that the line of symmetry passes through is black, then y can be fixed if the remaining two black corners are opposite each other (the diagram below will help you picture this). Hence ∣FixY(σ1)∣ = 6 (there are three elements of Y that are fixed for each of the two corners lying on the line of symmetry). The reflections σ2, σ3, σ4 are similar. Thus, ∣FixY(σi)∣ = 6 for i = 1, 2, 3, 4. Finally, we note that the reflections σ5, σ6, σ7, σ8 can never fix an element of Y , because their lines of symmetry will always divide the octagon into a half with two black corners, and a half with one black corner. Thus, ∣FixY(σi)∣ = 0 for i = 5, 6, 7, 8. Of course we also have that FixY(e) = Y, so ∣FixY(e)∣ = 56. Plugging all this into the Orbit Counting Theorem, we have, # orbits = 1 16 (56 + 0 ⋅ 7 + 6 ⋅ 4 + 0 ⋅ 4) = 5. Hence, the number of distinct necklaces that can be formed using precisely 3 black beads and 5 white beads is 5. Solution. (Question 9.5.10) Suppose Gx ∩ Gy /= ∅. We will prove that Gx = Gy. Since Gx ∩ Gy /= ∅, we can find z ∈ Gx ∩ Gy. Hence there is g1, g2 ∈ G such that λ(g1)x = z = λ(g2)y. Since λ is a homomorphism, λ(gi)−1 = λ(g−1 i ) for i = 1, 2. Therefore y = λ(g−1 2 g1)x ∈ Gx and x = λ(g−1 1 g2)y ∈ Gy. Since y ∈ Gx we have Gy ⊆ Gx, and since x ∈ Gy we have Gx ⊆ Gy. Hence Gx = Gy.
